result.summary: Medea, terrified that her aid to Jason has been discovered, flees her father's house, helps Jason charm the serpent and take the golden fleece, and sails with the Argonauts. Aeetes and his son Apsyrtus pursue them, and the heroes find a route by the Ister, where the Colchians cut them off and a truce is made over the fleece and Medea.

scenes.title: Medea flees the palace
scenes.summary: Medea, in terror, nearly poisons herself but is driven by Hera to flee. She says farewell to her home and runs through the night, watched and mocked by the moon.
scenes.stakes: Medea risks her father's wrath and exile, and nearly takes her own life in despair.

scenes.title: Medea joins the Argonauts
scenes.summary: Medea reaches the river and calls to Phrontis. Jason swears to marry her, and the crew take her aboard.
scenes.stakes: Medea stands to lose her family and honour if Jason abandons her.

scenes.title: Charming the serpent, seizing the fleece
scenes.summary: Medea lulls the serpent with song and drugs. Jason takes the fleece from the oak and they return to the heroes at dawn.
scenes.stakes: Jason and Medea face the sleepless serpent and discovery by gods or men.

scenes.title: Aeetes pursues the ship
scenes.summary: Jason rallies the crew. Aeetes and the Colchians pour out in pursuit, and Hera sends a wind that carries the Argo to the Halys.
scenes.stakes: Capture by Aeetes and the Colchian fleet would mean death and the loss of the fleece.

place.name: Phasis river mouth and Paphlagonian coast

scenes.title: Course to the Ister; truce
scenes.summary: Medea sacrifices to Hecate. Argus describes a new route by the Ister, and the Argo follows it as Apsyrtus cuts across to block them. A truce leaves Medea in Artemis's care.
scenes.stakes: The Argonauts risk defeat by a larger Colchian force and may lose Medea.

analysis.text: Medea's flight shows love and fear pulling her away from family and homeland, while Hera's will steers events.
Argus's geography of the Ister draws on Hellenistic scholarship and Egyptian lore about the extent of the known world.

legacy.text: Medea's flight and the fleece's theft shaped later treatments such as Euripides's Medea and Ovid's and Seneca's retellings.

fun_facts.text: Apollonius's claim that the Ister has a branch to the Adriatic reflects an ancient geographical belief that the Danube flowed into both the Black Sea and the Adriatic.

language_notes.text: The poet invokes the Muse at the opening of Book 4, as in epic tradition, asking her to tell Medea's story.
"Fill up the cup of woe" means she would soon suffer full, bitter consequences; 'forboded' is an old spelling of 'foreboded'.
"Made void the purposes of Hera": Hera wanted Medea alive to help Jason, so her suicide would have ruined the goddess's plan.
The bolts spring back by themselves, obeying Medea's magic song; 'self-moved' means moving without a hand.
"Titanian" marks the moon (Selene) as a child of the Titans, an older generation of gods.
The moon loves the sleeping shepherd Endymion, who lay in a cave on Mount Latmus ("Latinian" here). Medea's spells had often dragged the moon from her visits.
"The contest's issue" means the outcome of Jason's trial, the yoking of the fire-breathing bulls and the sowing of the dragon's teeth.
Phrontis and his brothers are sons of Phrixus, who came to Colchis on the golden ram, so they are Medea's nephews through her sister.
Clasping the knees is the gesture of a suppliant, asking for protection.
"All is brought to light" means her aid to Jason has been discovered; "nor doth any remedy come" means no cure or escape is left.
"Make me not a mark for blame" means do not let me become an object of reproach, since she has no kinsmen to defend her.
Hera is called queen of marriage because she presided over wedlock; Jason's oath by her makes the promise binding.
"Minyan" refers to the descendants of Minyas; here it describes Phrixus, who is carried by the Ram, and the Argonauts are also called Minyans.
"The alder of fugitives" is a rendering of Zeus's title as protector of exiles and those fleeing; Phrixus was a fugitive from Greece.
"Smirched" means smeared or stained; the altar is blackened by the soot of Phrixus's old sacrifice.
"Twain" is an archaic word for "two", here the two rivers Lycus and Phasis flowing together.
"Queen of the underworld, the night-wanderer" is Hecate, the goddess Medea invokes for her magic; she is not named in this sentence.
"Untempered charms" means unmixed, undiluted drugs; the brew is used at full strength.
"At the maiden bidding" is a slip for "maiden's bidding"; Medea tells Jason to take the fleece.
A "brocket" is a young stag in its second year, with its first small, unbranched horns.
"Ye" and "do ye" are archaic second-person plural forms; Jason addresses the whole crew, asking them to protect Medea.
"I ween" is archaic for "I think" or "I suppose"; "of a surety" means certainly.
Hellas is Greece; Achaea (sentence 55) is also used here for the Greek lands generally.
Hawsers are the thick ropes that moor a ship; cutting them frees the Argo.
"Who could reckon their tale?" means who could count their number; "tale" here is a tally.
"Thou wouldst not say" is the poet addressing the reader directly: you would not call it a fleet but a flock of birds.
"Pelasgian land" means Greece, named for the Pelasgians, an early people of the Greek lands. "Aeaean" marks Medea as from Aea, Aeetes' city.
The narrator refuses to describe the secret rite, a conventional reticence about mysteries; 'may no man know' means it is not for mortals to learn.
Phineus, the blind seer met earlier, gave the Argonauts vague directions for their return route, which they now try to interpret.
Tritonian Thebes means Egyptian Thebes, linking the priests' records to Egypt, which the passage treats as the source of ancient learning.
The Arcadians were proverbially older than the moon, an old Greek claim that they were among the earliest inhabitants of Greece.
Morning-land renders an old name for Egypt; the river Triton here is the Nile, whose flooding makes the land fertile without rain.
The unnamed king is the legendary Egyptian conqueror, usually identified with Sesostris, who was said to have settled colonists in Colchis.
Ister is the ancient name of the lower Danube; 'tilth' means ploughed or cultivated land.
The daughter of Zeus is Artemis; the Colchians spare her islands out of reverence, which is why the Argonauts can land there.
Minyae is the name for the Argonauts, descended from the legendary Minyas; Leto's daughter is Artemis, who is to hold Medea in safekeeping.

context_notes.text: Aeetes is king of Colchis and Medea's father. Jason has just completed his impossible tasks with her secret help, so Aeetes plots revenge.
The sons of Phrixus are Medea's nephews, children of her sister Chalciope. They are allied with the Argonauts.
Medea is a priestess of Hecate, a goddess of witchcraft, and gathers drugs and herbs for her magic. The temple she heads for is probably Hecate's.
Aeson's son is Jason, who leads the Argonauts. The epithet identifies him by his father.
The guardian serpent is the dragon that never sleeps and watches over the golden fleece hanging in the sacred grove.
Phrixus fled on the golden ram from his stepmother, reached Colchis, sacrificed the ram to Zeus and hung its fleece in the grove of Ares.
The serpent was the sleepless guardian of the fleece, which hung in the grove sacred to Ares.
The grove of Ares was the god of war's sacred precinct, where the fleece was kept.
Helios is the sun god and father of Aeetes. His divine horses explain the king's speed and splendour.
Apsyrtus is Medea's young brother, son of Aeetes. His presence in the chariot foreshadows his later fate in the poem.
Aeetes appeals to Helios and Zeus as divine witnesses, as oath-keepers and protectors of justice, to the wrong done him.
Hera favours Jason and protects the Argonauts. Pelias is the king who sent Jason on the quest and will be destroyed through Medea.
Hecate was a goddess of magic, night and crossroads, whom Medea serves as priestess; she offers sacrifice to her before the new route.
Apsyrtus is Medea's brother and leads the Colchian fleet pursuing the Argonauts to recover her and the fleece.
The truce settles the quarrel by arbitration: the Argonauts keep the fleece, while Medea is held by Artemis until a king decides her fate.

literary_notes.text: Medea's trembling is compared to a fawn terrified by hounds, stressing her helplessness and fear.
Medea is likened to a young bondmaid fleeing a harsh mistress, showing her as vulnerable and unused to hardship.
The moon addresses Medea directly, and this also gives the moon a mocking, human voice.
The moon's warning of a burden of pain and many sighs foreshadows Medea's suffering to come.
"Thrice she called, and thrice" balances call and answer, and the ritual number conveys urgency and the tension of the night.
The short, balanced line "Word and deed were one" sums up the crew's instant, unified action after the long speeches.
Medea's backward start and outstretched hands show her doubt and grief at leaving home, contrasting with the crew's eager haste.
The opening compares the hour to hunters who avoid dawn's light, setting the time of the scene with a vivid image from daily life.
The fleece is likened to a cloud reddened by sunrise, conveying its glowing, otherworldly gold before we see it up close.
The serpent's coils are compared to smoke rising in wavering wreaths from a smouldering fire, stressing their endless, rolling motion.
The relaxing coils are likened to a dark wave rolling soundlessly over a sluggish sea, showing the charm taking effect.
Jason's delight in the fleece is compared to a girl who sees moonlight on her robe, giving the hero a gentle, almost tender image.
The fleece gleams like the lightning of Zeus, tying the object's brilliance to divine power.
Jason raises the stakes by tying the voyage to families, country and all Hellas, making the crew's effort a matter of shared fate.
The Colchian host is compared to waves and to autumn leaves, stressing overwhelming numbers; the poet breaks off with a rhetorical question.
The ships are compared to a flock of birds, conveying their number and noisy, swarming speed.
Calling Medea "a bane to the house of Pelias" anticipates the vengeance she will bring on Pelias.
The poet speaks in the first person, claiming religious awe, and points to a surviving altar to give the story the authority of present-day evidence.
The trail of heavenly light shows divine favour guiding the heroes, marking the route as sanctioned by the gods.
The shepherds mistake the ships for sea monsters, showing how new and strange the Argo appears to people who have never seen seafaring vessels.
